description_full: Seneca Foods Corporation provides packaged fruits and vegetables in the United States and internationally. The company offers canned, frozen, and jarred fruits and vegetables; and packaged snack chips and other food products under the private label, as well as under various national and regional brands that the company owns or licenses, including Aunt Nellie's, CherryMan, Green Giant, Green Valley, Libby's, READ, and Seneca. In addition, it packs canned and frozen vegetables. Further, the company engages in the sale of cans, ends, and seeds, as well as aircraft operations. It provides its products to grocery outlets, including supermarkets, mass merchandisers, limited assortment stores, club stores, and dollar stores; specialty retailers; and food service distributors, restaurant chains, industrial markets, other food packagers, and export customers in approximately 55 countries, as well as federal, state, and local governments for school and other feeding programs. Seneca Foods Corporation was incorporated in 1949 and is headquartered in Fairport, New York.

financial_summary: Seneca Foods Corp. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $1.0B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 7% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 8% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $298M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 8.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -24.9% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.61x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 69% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 13% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 0.51, it is more defensive than the market.
About $16.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 37% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 73% below its DCF fair value of $555, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $406 to $790 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 8.7 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 5.8 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 3.4 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 114% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 29.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $202 on average, 34% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% earns above the cost of capital of 6.7%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.02).
It runs a 8% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-24.9% of assets).
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($42.7M of cash against $369.9M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
Working capital ties up about 165 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.5% over 3 years and 2.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 2.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.7% on average.
own: Insiders own 13.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 80%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 1 sale over the past year, net $323K sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.1% (1.1% in buybacks).
people: With about 2,900 employees, each generates about $544K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $103K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.2M (2x revenue per employee).
